title: Bobble stitch — the raised cluster on a flat background
subtitle: Five trebles into one stitch, joined at the top and pushed to the public side
excerpt: Bobble stitch is a cluster of trebles worked into the same base stitch and closed together at the top. The cluster puffs out on the side facing away from you as you work — so for right-side-out rows, work bobbles on the wrong-side row.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 5 (1890) — raised cluster stitches in textured crochet fabric. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — cluster techniques in crochet.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cluster of trebles (usually five) worked into the same base stitch with each treble left incomplete until all are joined at the top in one yarn-over. The cluster pops out on the side facing away from you as you work.

content.text: is a cluster of five trebles worked into the same base stitch, each left unfinished until all five are joined at the top with one yarn-over. The cluster pops out on the back — the side facing away from you as you work. For a blanket or cushion worked flat with right-side rows facing, work the bobbles on the wrong-side rows.

attrs.title: Bobble vs popcorn vs puff
attrs.body: Bobble: unfinished trebles closed together at the top — the cluster pushes to the far side. Popcorn: complete trebles worked into the same stitch, then the first stitch removed-from-hook is threaded back and the top pulled through — the cluster pushes to the near side. Puff: elongated half trebles pulled up and drawn together — softer than both. Each has a distinct look; the terms are sometimes used interchangeably but the methods differ.

content.text: Work to the base stitch where the bobble goes.
Yarn over, insert into the base stitch, yarn over and pull up a loop, yarn over and pull through two — two loops remain. This is one incomplete treble.
Repeat step 2 into the same base stitch four more times — six loops on the hook (one from each of the five incomplete trebles, plus the original loop on the hook).
Yarn over and pull through all six loops at once. One chain to close (optional — some patterns call it, some don't). One bobble made.
Continue along the row. The bobble faces away from you. Turn at the end of the row — the bobbles now face the right side.

Bobbles are usually spaced with 2-3 double crochet stitches between each one so the fabric lies flat. A bobble row alternates with plain rows to keep the structure even. All-over bobble stitch (every alternate stitch, every alternate row) makes a heavily textured fabric — generous on yarn.

items.symptom: Bobbles face the wrong side after turning
items.cause: Working bobbles on the right-side row instead of the wrong-side row
items.fix: Bobbles push toward the back. Work them on wrong-side rows so they push toward the public side. If working in the round, push each bobble to the outside with a finger as you close.

items.cause: Tension too loose, or all six loops not pulled through cleanly
items.fix: Pull through all six loops at once firmly. An optional closing chain helps lock the bobble. Slightly tighter tension on the bobble stitch itself (not the whole row) keeps the cluster round.

items.symptom: Fabric pulls in at the bobble rows
items.cause: Too many stitches clustered into one base stitch pulls the fabric tight at that point
items.fix: Work into the stitch loosely — five trebles into one base stitch needs room. Use a slightly looser tension than the plain rows, or go up one hook size for bobble rows.

content.text: Popcorn stitch is the cleaner-edged version — the cluster pops toward the working side and each popcorn sits more defined. Puff stitch uses elongated half trebles and gives a softer, rounded bloom.
